reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A leading cause of blindness in working-age adults and directly related to duration of diabetes and quality of glycaemic control
Early (non-proliferative) disease is usually asymptomatic, underscoring the value of regular screening fundus photography
Non-proliferative signs include microaneurysms, dot-and-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, and venous beading
Proliferative disease is defined by neovascularisation of the disc or retina, which risks vitreous haemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment
Diabetic maculopathy (macular oedema) is the commonest cause of visual loss and can occur at any stage
Anti-VEGF intravitreal therapy is first-line for centre-involving macular oedema, while panretinal laser photocoagulation is used for proliferative disease
Blood pressure, lipid, and glycaemic control materially slow progression alongside ophthalmic treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic hyperglycaemia damages retinal capillaries through pathways including accumulation of advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress, and pericyte loss. This weakens vessel walls (forming microaneurysms), increases permeability (causing exudation and macular oedema), and causes capillary occlusion leading to retinal ischaemia. Ischaemic retina releases vascular endothelial growth factor and other mediators that drive pathological new-vessel formation; these fragile vessels bleed and contract, producing vitreous haemorrhage and tractional detachment in advanced proliferative disease.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundoscopy and fundus photography for screening and staging
Optical coherence tomography to detect and quantify macular oedema
Fluorescein angiography to map ischaemia and neovascularisation
Systemic review of HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids, and renal function
redFlags: Sudden visual loss or floaters suggesting vitreous haemorrhage
New vessels on the disc or elsewhere indicating sight-threatening proliferative disease
Centre-involving macular oedema threatening central vision
Rubeosis iridis (iris new vessels) heralding neovascular glaucoma
reference.prognosis: With timely screening, good systemic control, and prompt laser or anti-VEGF treatment, most severe visual loss is preventable; neglected proliferative disease and macular oedema carry a high risk of blindness.
pitfalls: Assuming good vision means no retinopathy and skipping screening
Missing macular oedema that requires OCT rather than fundoscopy alone to detect
Rapid tightening of glycaemic control causing transient worsening of retinopathy
Overlooking pregnancy as an accelerator of progression
management: Optimise systemic control of glycaemia, blood pressure and lipids to slow progression and reduce sight-threatening disease
Enrol in regular screening fundus photography to detect asymptomatic disease and stage progression
Treat centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy as first line, with intravitreal corticosteroid as an alternative
Treat proliferative disease with panretinal laser photocoagulation to induce regression of neovascularisation
Refer for vitreoretinal surgery with vitrectomy for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment
Monitor visual acuity and use optical coherence tomography to guide macular oedema treatment
Refer promptly to ophthalmology for any proliferative change, maculopathy or sudden visual loss
